A promise renewed

In 1868 the Fourteenth Amendment promised every person "the equal protection of the laws." For nearly a century, segregation laws and violence broke that promise across the South. In the twenty years after the Second World War, Black Americans and their allies forced the nation to keep it.

In this unit you will read the Constitution and the Supreme Court on "separate but equal," analyze the laws and speeches that ended legal segregation, research one grassroots campaign, and argue which moment was the movement's most important turning point.

This is the unit where our semester question, who receives the full rights of citizenship, is answered most directly. Watch how ordinary people, courts, presidents and Congress each played a part, and ask which mattered most.

Key terms: equal protection, segregation, Jim Crow, desegregation, civil disobedience, boycott, sit-in, filibuster, public accommodation, poll tax, literacy test.
title: Equal Protection
